case_study_insert.main_stem: Vale & Wren Xpress (VWX) is a public limited company in the fast-fashion e-commerce sector, employing a workforce of 240. Founded in 2007 by Dominic Vale in Singapore, the business sells low-cost clothing through mobile apps and 30 stores and operates a hierarchical structure with centralised, autocratic leadership. VWX plans to invest $1.8 million in an automated e-commerce distribution centre, financed by a $1.0 million share issue and an $800,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $660,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.50 a unit and a selling price of $19.50, and sells 120,000 units a year. VWX faces two operational problems: a 3.6% garment defect rate and labour turnover of 18%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — Q4 2026: The automated packing line handled 31,000 orders, of which 3.6% failed inspection, down from 5.1%. Customer complaints rose to 412, average delivery took 5.6 days, and the stock-record error rate was 1.9%. Labour turnover reached 18% and 34 of the 240 staff left during the quarter; exit interviews showed 61% cited repetitive work. A job rotation scheme would cost $180 a worker to train. Installing an inspection station costs $24,000, while a supplier quality assurance programme would cost $90,000 a year.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Vale & Wren Xpress as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (January 2027): (1) The base interest rate has risen from 5.5% to 6.25%, increasing the cost of the $800,000 variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise 7.1% from $13.82 to $14.80 an hour from April 2027, affecting the 240-strong workforce. (3) Cotton and synthetic fabric input costs have risen 13.5% year-on-year, while consumer spending on fast fashion fell 3.2% over the same period.

questions.question_text: VWX plans to finance its $1.8 million automated e-commerce distribution centre with a $1.0 million share issue. Explain two advantages for VWX of using the share issue rather than borrowing an extra $1.0 million.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue brings $1.0 million of permanent capital with no interest or repayment schedule, easing pressure on the existing $800,000 bank loan and on fixed costs of $660,000 a year. The cash can be directed at the automated e-commerce distribution centre instead of servicing debt, helping VWX handle the 3.6% defect rate and the 5.6-day delivery time without raising the $19.50 selling price.

Point 2: Issuing shares strengthens the balance sheet and lowers reliance on lenders, so the public limited company is less exposed if interest rates rise or consumer spending on fast fashion falls 3.2%. Unlike another loan, equity does not require collateral over the $1.8 million centre. The trade-off is dilution of existing shareholders and possible dividend pressure, but given a 18% labour turnover problem and 412 complaints, VWX needs cash flexibility more than the preservation of every existing shareholding percentage. Equity also absorbs losses if the 3.6% defect rate is not fixed quickly, whereas loan interest would still be due; this protects the $1.8 million centre in its first year.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to VWX's funding decision and expansion.

questions.question_text: VWX is promoting its low-cost clothing range. Consider mobile app notifications, celebrity endorsement, or national television advertising. Which should VWX choose to promote the range? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Mobile app notifications: VWX already sells through mobile apps, so push messages and in-app offers can reach existing buyers instantly and drive repeat orders towards the 120,000-unit target. The cost is low and offers can be targeted by past purchases, which helps when 3.2% less is being spent on fast fashion. The limitation is that notifications only reach people who have installed the app, so they cannot easily attract new customers.

Celebrity endorsement: A well-chosen celebrity could generate rapid awareness and social media coverage for low-cost fashion, helping VWX compete for attention and supporting the $1.8 million distribution centre's volume. However, fees are high and unpredictable, and if the celebrity's image clashes with the brand or a scandal occurs, the $19.50 range loses credibility; it also says little about quality when 3.6% of garments fail inspection.

National television advertising: TV gives the widest reach and can build mass awareness across the 30 stores and the apps, which suits a public limited company with 240 staff. Yet airtime and production are very expensive relative to a $660,000 annual fixed-cost base, and much of the audience will not buy online fashion, so wastage would be high.

Recommendation: VWX should choose mobile app notifications, backed by small social promotions. They are cheap, measurable and use the existing app channel to protect contribution on 120,000 units; celebrity endorsement is rejected as costly and risky when a 3.6% defect rate needs fixing first, and television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted. VWX can add wider advertising once the 18% labour turnover and complaint levels are under control.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of VWX with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of VWX with a well-justified recommendation explaining why celebrity endorsement and television lose.

questions.question_text: VWX's labour turnover has reached 18% and 61% of leavers cited repetitive work. Explain two benefits for VWX of introducing job rotation.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Job rotation moves the workforce of 240 between packing, inspection and stock-recording tasks, which directly addresses the 61% of leavers who cited repetitive work. Greater variety should raise motivation and reduce the 18% labour turnover, cutting the disruption caused by 34 staff leaving in one quarter and lowering recruitment and induction costs for a business with fixed costs of $660,000 a year.

Point 2: Rotation also builds multi-skilled staff who can cover the automated e-commerce distribution centre when demand spikes, improving the 5.6-day delivery time and helping maintain output of 120,000 units. Workers who have performed inspection are more likely to spot the 3.6% garment defects, while the $180 per worker training cost is small beside the $1.8 million investment. Under the hierarchical structure, managers can schedule rotation to keep the centralised autocratic leadership's standards consistent across the 30 stores and the packing line. Management must still schedule rotation so that inspection remains independent, otherwise the 3.6% defect rate and the 1.9% stock-record errors could be missed.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to VWX's turnover, complaints and volume.

questions.question_text: VWX wants to cut its 3.6% garment defect rate. Consider installing an inspection station or introducing a supplier quality assurance programme. Which should VWX choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Installing an inspection station: At $24,000 this is a one-off cost that catches faulty garments before they are packed, directly reducing the 3.6% failure rate recorded across 31,000 orders and limiting the 412 customer complaints. Inspectors can give immediate feedback on the packing line and the cost is small against the $1.8 million distribution centre. Its weakness is that it detects defects after production, so waste has already occurred, and it does nothing to address the 1.9% stock-record error rate or supplier quality.

Supplier quality assurance programme: Costing $90,000 a year, this sets standards with suppliers and prevents poor material entering production, which can tackle the source of the 3.6% defects and reduce rework. Because 5.1% of garments previously failed inspection, prevention could produce a lasting fall. The recurring $90,000 is larger than the inspection station's $24,000, however, and it will not catch packing mistakes inside VWX itself.

Decision: VWX should install the inspection station first and add a limited supplier quality assurance programme once defect data identifies which suppliers are at fault. The $24,000 one-off cost gives immediate control over the 3.6% defects and 412 complaints, whereas committing $90,000 a year before diagnosing the cause is rejected as premature. Supplier assurance is not abandoned: it is deferred until inspection records show whether defects originate with suppliers, at which point prevention becomes the better long-term tool. VWX should set a target for the 3.6% defect rate and review the 31,000-order log monthly, judging the $24,000 purchase on whether complaints fall from the current 412.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two quality approaches with limited application to VWX.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both approaches in the context of VWX.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both approaches in the context of VWX with a well-justified decision covering cost, timing and defect prevention.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how VWX's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $660,000 ÷ ($19.50 − $8.50) = $660,000 ÷ $11.00 = 60,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 60,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $19.50 − $8.50 = $11.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $11.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways VWX's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Break-even output of 60,000 units against sales of 120,000 units leaves a margin of safety of 60,000 units, showing how far fast-fashion demand can fall before the $1.8 million distribution centre stops contributing.
2. Contribution per unit of $11.00 lets managers test a price promotion: cutting $1.00 to $18.50 leaves $10.00, so an illustrative 10% rise in volume (12,000 units) would add 12,000 × $10.00 = $120,000 of contribution, enough to cover the $90,000 quality programme.
3. The 60,000-unit break-even target helps decide whether the $800,000 bank loan can be serviced from profits before further expansion of the 30 stores.
4. Unit cost of $14.00 ($660,000 ÷ 120,000 units = $5.50 plus $8.50 variable cost) is a benchmark to track the 3.6% defect rate and 5.6-day delivery performance each quarter.

questions.model_answer: (i) break-even output = 60,000 units | (ii) contribution per unit = $11.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 60,000 units against 120,000-unit sales; a $1.00 price promotion on $11.00 contribution; servicing the $800,000 bank loan; unit cost of $14.00 to monitor 3.6% defects.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate VWX's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has VWX's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.25 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.40 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.80 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.00 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $180,000 + $220,000 + $100,000 = $500,000; 2025 current assets = $152,000 + $250,000 + $130,000 = $532,000. Dividing by current liabilities of $400,000 in 2024 and $380,000 in 2025 gives the first pair of figures. Removing stock leaves $320,000 in 2024 and $380,000 in 2025, and dividing those by the same liabilities gives the second pair.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved on both measures. The first ratio rose from 1.25 to 1.40 because current assets grew while current liabilities fell from $400,000 to $380,000, giving a wider cushion for the $1.8 million distribution centre commitments. The second ratio improved from 0.80 to 1.00, so VWX no longer depends on selling its $152,000 of inventories to meet short-term debts — important when the 3.6% defect rate and falling fast-fashion spending could leave stock slow to move. However, trade receivables increased from $220,000 to $250,000, tying up cash that could fund the $24,000 inspection station, and the $800,000 bank loan still carries interest risk.

Conclusion: VWX's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher and the rise in the second measure shows the improvement does not rely on inventory. The remaining weakness is growing receivables, so management should tighten credit control before the 18% labour turnover and new centre place further strain on cash. The finance team should track the $130,000 cash balance monthly, since a $24,000 inspection station and a $90,000 quality programme would compete for the same short-term funds.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether VWX's position improved.

questions.question_text: VWX is investing in an automated e-commerce distribution centre. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for VWX of this investment.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Automation can process the 31,000 monthly orders faster and more accurately than manual labour, reducing the 5.6-day delivery time and the 1.9% stock-record error rate while supporting 120,000 units a year. It also reduces dependence on staff in a business where labour turnover is 18% and 34 workers left in one quarter, protecting the $1.8 million investment's output and the $11.00 contribution on each garment.

Disadvantage: The $1.8 million outlay requires a $1.0 million share issue and an $800,000 bank loan, creating dilution and interest obligations on top of fixed costs of $660,000 a year. With a 3.6% defect rate and 412 complaints, automation may simply deliver faulty garments faster unless the $24,000 inspection station is also funded; and if consumer spending on fast fashion falls 3.2%, the new capacity could be underused, so VWX must check utilisation before expanding further. With 412 complaints and a 1.9% stock-record error rate, the centre should be introduced alongside better inspection rather than treated as a complete answer to service problems.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to VWX's volume, labour turnover and funding.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 6.25%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 13.5% rise in cotton and synthetic fabric costs will affect VWX. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.5% to 6.25%): Because the bulletin specifies a variable-rate $800,000 loan, the extra interest is 0.75% of $800,000 = $6,000 a year (0.0075 × $800,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $660,000 a year, and VWX can cap it by fixing the rate, so this is the smallest direct cost change even though higher rates may add to the 3.2% fall in fast-fashion spending.

Minimum wage rise (7.1%, to $14.80 an hour): The insert gives a workforce of 240 but no hours worked or pay rates, so an annual wage bill cannot honestly be invented. Qualitatively the rise increases distribution and store costs and is unavoidable. Its effect depends on the 120,000 units sold: with labour turnover already 18% and 61% of leavers citing repetitive work, a wage rise is only affordable if job rotation holds productivity, otherwise unit labour cost climbs and narrows the $11.00 contribution.

Fabric cost inflation (13.5%): The insert states a $8.50 variable cost per unit but does not break it into materials and other elements. The honest upper bound is 0.135 × $8.50 = $1.1475 per unit, which across 120,000 units is $137,700 a year (120,000 × $1.1475). Even if only part of variable cost is fabric, the increase recurs on every garment and directly attacks the $11.00 contribution that must cover $660,000 fixed costs and service the $1.8 million centre.

Conclusion: The 13.5% fabric cost rise will have the greatest impact. It can reach roughly $137,700 a year, far above the $6,000 interest change, and unlike the wage rise it can be bounded from the insert and hits every unit sold. The interest rise is small and fixable, while the wage effect cannot be quantified and depends on productivity, so both rank below input inflation. VWX should renegotiate fabric contracts and use the $24,000 inspection station to avoid wasting expensive material on the 3.6% of faulty garments.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to VWX.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on VWX's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of VWX with a well-justified judgement that fabric cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
